questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Two organisms share a genus but belong to different species. A third is in a different genus of the same family. Which pair is guaranteed to share the most specific named rank?
options: A) First two: genus; all three: family
B) First two: family; all three: order
C) First two: species; all three: genus
D) All three: genus and species
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) The first two share a genus, and all three share a family.
Why: A species is nested within a genus, and genera are nested within a family. Different species do not share a species designation; the third organism's different genus leaves family as the most specific rank common to all three. This uses the stated ranks, without assuming that close resemblance changes formal placement.
Why not the others: (B) downgrades the first pair despite their shared genus; (C) incorrectly merges different species and genera; (D) places the third in a genus explicitly excluded.
Key point: Compare the lowest common rank in a nested hierarchy.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.topic: Structural Organisation In Plants And Animals
questions.question: A transverse root section in the figure has a central star-shaped xylem, phloem between its arms, and no conspicuous central pith. Another section has many xylem-phloem units around a large pith. Which assignment follows from both clues?
options: A) Both monocot roots at different ages
B) First monocot stem; second dicot stem
C) First dicot root; second monocot root
D) First dicot stem; second monocot root
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) The first is a dicot root and the second a monocot root.
Why: Radial vascular tissue with xylem arms alternating with phloem establishes root anatomy. A small or absent central pith and a few xylem arms typify the dicot root; numerous alternating strands around a developed pith support the monocot root. The centre and arrangement must be read together, not a single coloured region.
Why not the others: (A) treats the large pith and many vascular units as an age effect; (B) misreads the first radial stele as a stem; (D) misreads the first section as a dicot stem despite its radial root pattern.
Key point: Use both vascular arrangement and pith.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: In a translation experiment, a ribosome moves along an mRNA from its start codon. A mutation introduces a stop codon after 48 sense codons; the original stop followed 75 sense codons. How many fewer amino acids are incorporated, assuming no other change?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 27 fewer amino acids.
Given: The normal message has 75 sense codons before its stop codon. The mutant has a stop codon after 48 sense codons.
Formula/Principle: Each sense codon adds one amino acid; a stop codon adds none and ends translation.
Step 1: Normal polypeptide = 75 amino acids.
Step 2: Mutant polypeptide = 48 amino acids.
Step 3: Difference = 75 − 48 = 27.
Why: The ribosome reads the message three bases at a time from the start codon and stops at the first stop codon in the reading frame. A premature stop codon (a nonsense mutation) releases the chain early, so every codon after it is left unread, even though those codons are unchanged.
Why not the others: (A) 26 counts one of the stop codons as if it added or removed an amino acid. (C) 28 adds an extra residue for the same reason in the other direction. (D) 75 is the length of the normal protein, not the number of amino acids lost.
Key point: Protein length = number of sense codons between the start and the first in-frame stop, counting the start codon.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Isolated thylakoids are illuminated with electron transport operating, but a membrane-permeable proton carrier is added. Oxygen evolution continues briefly while ATP synthesis drops. Which direct change best explains the decoupling?
options: A) The carrier collapses the proton gradient across the thylakoid membrane
B) The carrier prevents water from donating electrons to PSII
C) The carrier removes the ADP substrate from the stroma
D) The carrier makes ATP synthase a source of photons
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) The carrier dissipates the transmembrane proton gradient.
Why: Electron flow can still oxidise water and release oxygen, while the carrier allows protons to return without passing through ATP synthase. The resulting loss of proton motive force deprives ATP synthase of its driving gradient. A short period of oxygen evolution is consistent with an electron path that has not itself been blocked.
Why not the others: (B) would stop oxygen formation directly; (C) is not a membrane carrier's action; (D) reverses the energy conversion of ATP synthase.
Key point: Separate electron transport from coupling through the proton gradient.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: A patient's circulating thyroxine falls after reduced thyroid output, while the hypothalamus and pituitary remain functional. Which immediate feedback response is expected before treatment?
options: A) TRH falls and TSH rises
B) TRH and TSH both tend to rise
C) TRH rises and TSH falls
D) TRH and TSH both tend to fall
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Both TRH and TSH tend to rise.
Why: Thyroxine normally inhibits hypothalamic TRH and pituitary TSH through negative feedback. A fall in thyroid hormone removes part of this inhibition at both upstream levels, so the intact axis increases drive to the thyroid. The premise rules out a primary pituitary failure, which would change the inference.
Why not the others: (A) applies inhibition to the hypothalamus despite low hormone; (C) inhibits TSH in the wrong direction; (D) is the usual response to excess rather than deficient thyroid hormone.
Key point: Follow the direction of negative feedback.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: The diagram shows pollen from plant P placed on two stigmas: its own stigma and a genetically different stigma of the same species. Both grains hydrate, but tubes grow only in the latter style. Which mechanism first separates the outcomes?
options: A) Absence of viable pollen grains on either stigma
B) Failure of pollen dispersal from the anther
C) Self-incompatibility recognition after pollen deposition
D) Embryo abortion after double fertilisation
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Self-incompatibility blocks tube growth on the self stigma.
Why: Hydration confirms that pollen arrived and was initially viable on both stigmas. The first observed divergence is tube growth within the style; a genetically controlled pollen-pistil interaction can reject self pollen at or after germination while accepting compatible pollen of the same species. The diagram distinguishes arrival from successful fertilisation.
Why not the others: (B) contradicts deposition on both stigmas; (A) contradicts hydration and the successful cross; (D) occurs far later and cannot explain absent pollen tubes.
Key point: Locate the earliest incompatible step in the pollen-pistil pathway.
questions.image_alt: Self and cross pollen on two stigmas; hydrated grains on both, tubes only in the cross style.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: A replication fork advances rightward. The top parental strand is labelled 3′ at its left end and 5′ at its right end. Which new strand is synthesised continuously along that top template toward the fork?
options: A) No strand; the top template cannot be copied
B) A strand extending 3′ to 5′ toward the right
C) A strand extending 5′ to 3′ toward the left
D) A strand extending 5′ to 3′ toward the right
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) A new 5′ to 3′ strand extends rightward.
Why: DNA polymerase reads the top template in the 3′ to 5′ direction as it travels right, adding nucleotides to the 3′ end of the complementary strand. Its 5′ to 3′ synthesis therefore keeps pace with the rightward fork. Direction is fixed by template polarity, not by which strand is drawn above the other.
Why not the others: (B) violates polymerase synthesis polarity; (C) describes synthesis away from this fork; (A) ignores complementarity and the available template.
Key point: Read template 3′ to 5′ to determine leading-strand direction.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Before an antibiotic is applied, a bacterial culture contains a rare resistant variant. After several generations under the drug, most survivors are resistant. Which additional observation would directly reject the claim that the drug created the resistant mutation only after exposure?
options: A) The same resistance allele is detected in archived cells collected before exposure
B) The resistant population grows slowly without the drug
C) The drug inhibits a susceptible enzyme
D) The final population has fewer total cells
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) The allele was present before treatment.
Why: Detection of the identical resistance allele in an archived pretreatment sample establishes that the variant preceded the selection pressure. Antibiotic exposure can enrich this pre-existing variant because susceptible cells die or divide less. Growth differences after treatment do not establish when the mutation first arose.
Why not the others: (B) concerns fitness cost, not mutation timing; (C) describes drug action but not origin of the allele; (D) records population size without revealing ancestry.
Key point: A pre-exposure control separates selection from induced origin.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Why PCR uses a thermostable DNA polymerase
questions.question: Each cycle of PCR includes a denaturation step at about 94 °C. Why is the DNA polymerase from Thermus aquaticus (Taq polymerase) used instead of an ordinary DNA polymerase from E. coli?
options: A) Taq polymerase needs no primers to begin synthesis
B) Taq polymerase works without deoxynucleotides
C) Taq polymerase stays active after repeated heating, so it need not be added again in every cycle
D) Taq polymerase cuts the DNA at specific recognition sequences
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Taq polymerase stays active after repeated heating, so it need not be added again in every cycle.
Why: Each PCR cycle heats the mixture to about 94 °C to separate the DNA strands. An ordinary polymerase would be denatured at that temperature and would have to be replaced after every cycle. Thermus aquaticus lives in hot springs, and its polymerase keeps its shape and activity at high temperature. One addition of the enzyme therefore lasts through all the cycles, which is what makes automated PCR practical.
Why not the others: (A) Taq polymerase, like every DNA polymerase, can only extend an existing 3′ end, so primers are still needed. (B) It builds DNA from deoxynucleotides and cannot work without them. (D) Cutting DNA at recognition sequences is the job of restriction endonucleases, not of a polymerase.
Key point: PCR steps: denaturation, primer annealing, extension by a thermostable polymerase.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: A population grows logistically with carrying capacity K. At one census it has N=K/2; in an otherwise identical habitat another population has N=K. Which has greater instantaneous per-capita growth rate under the same intrinsic rate r?
options: C) Both are equal and positive
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) The per-capita rate is higher at half the carrying capacity.
Why: The logistic model gives \(\frac{1}{N}\frac{dN}{dt}=r(1-N/K)\). At \(K/2\) the factor is \(1/2\), whereas at \(K\) it is zero because density limitation balances growth. This asks for growth per individual, not the total change in population size.
Why not the others: (A) ignores zero net growth at capacity; (C) assumes density has no effect; (D) incorrectly transfers the capacity boundary to half capacity.
Key point: Divide logistic growth by N before comparing per-capita rates.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: A bacterial operon reporter is expressed when an inducer is present. A strain lacking the repressor gene expresses the reporter even without inducer; restoring the repressor gene restores inducibility. Which conclusion is supported?
options: A) The repressor is necessary for transcription in all conditions
B) The inducer directly removes RNA polymerase from DNA
C) The reporter gene is deleted in the mutant
D) The repressor normally inhibits transcription without inducer
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Repressor action keeps the operon off without inducer.
Why: The deletion is a loss-of-function comparison: expression without inducer appears when repressor is absent and the inducible pattern returns when it is restored. That rescue links the phenotype to repressor-mediated negative control, rather than an unrelated mutation. It does not by itself identify every molecular contact of the inducer.
Why not the others: (B) predicts decreased expression on induction; (C) conflicts with the reporter signal; (A) conflicts with expression in the repressor-null strain.
Key point: Use a knockout and restoration together to infer regulatory direction.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: An mRNA coding segment is 5′-AUG UUU GGA UAA-3′. A single base change converts UUU to UUC. With the standard code, which outcome follows?
options: A) The same amino acid is encoded at the second position
B) Translation stops at the second codon
C) The reading frame shifts by one nucleotide
D) A different amino acid is necessarily incorporated
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Both UUU and UUC encode phenylalanine.
Why: Reading begins at AUG and proceeds in non-overlapping triplets. The substitution changes the third base of the second codon, but these two triplets are synonymous in the standard genetic code; subsequent GGA and the UAA stop stay in frame. A base change need not change protein sequence.
Why not the others: (B) confuses UUC with a stop codon; (C) requires an insertion or deletion, not a substitution; (D) ignores codon degeneracy.
Key point: Translate the altered codon before predicting protein effects.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: During an isometric skeletal-muscle contraction, a sarcomere develops tension while its overall length is held fixed. Which molecular event still occurs?
options: A) Thin filaments themselves contract in length
C) Myosin heads cycle on actin and consume ATP
D) Z discs must move closer together
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Cross-bridge cycling can generate force without net shortening.
Why: Isometric means the externally measured sarcomere length is held fixed, not that contractile proteins become inactive. Actin-myosin attachment, power strokes and ATP-dependent detachment can continue against an opposing load while net displacement remains zero. Thick and thin filament lengths do not change during sliding-filament action.
Why not the others: (B) changes thick-filament length; (A) changes actin length; (D) would indicate shortening rather than the stated fixed length.
Key point: Separate force generation from net movement.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Bivalents and chromatids in meiosis I
questions.question: A diploid cell has 2n=16 and enters meiosis after normal DNA replication. How many bivalents are present at prophase I, and how many chromatids are present in the cell at metaphase I?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 8 bivalents and 32 chromatids.
Given: 2n = 16, so there are 8 pairs of homologous chromosomes. DNA has replicated before meiosis.
Formula/Principle: A bivalent is one pair of synapsed homologous chromosomes. After replication each chromosome has two chromatids.
Step 1: Number of bivalents = number of homologous pairs = 16 ÷ 2 = 8.
Step 2: Chromatids = 16 chromosomes × 2 = 32.
Step 3: Homologues do not separate until anaphase I, so all 32 chromatids are still in the cell at metaphase I.
Why: In prophase I the two homologues of each pair come together, so the 16 chromosomes are seen as 8 units. Each unit is a tetrad of four chromatids, and 8 × 4 = 32 gives the same total. Nothing has yet been distributed to daughter cells at metaphase I.
Why not the others: (A) 16 bivalents counts every chromosome as a bivalent instead of every pair. (C) 16 chromatids forgets that DNA replication doubled the chromatids. (D) 4 bivalents and 16 chromatids would describe a cell with 2n = 8.
Key point: Bivalents = n; chromatids in meiosis I = 4n.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.topic: Structural Organisation In Plants And Animals
questions.question: A young dicot stem is wounded around the vascular bundles. The surviving cells between adjacent bundles divide to form a continuous cambial ring. Which tissue provided those connecting cambial segments?
options: C) Cork cells outside the cortex
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Interfascicular parenchyma contributes the connecting cambium.
Why: Within a bundle the original cambium is intrafascicular. Between bundles, living parenchyma cells regain division capacity and form interfascicular cambium, joining the segments into a continuous ring for secondary growth. The question specifically concerns the bridge between vascular bundles rather than the pre-existing cambium inside one bundle.
Why not the others: (B) has dead vessel elements unsuitable for division; (C) lies outside the relevant ring; (A) is a specialised conducting element, not the intervening parenchyma.
Key point: Identify where secondary meristem arises between bundles.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Bond order from molecular orbital theory
questions.question: Using molecular orbital theory, which of the species O₂⁺, O₂, O₂⁻ and O₂²⁻ has the highest bond order?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) O₂⁺.
Why: In molecular orbital theory, O₂ (16 electrons) has 10 bonding and 6 antibonding electrons, so its bond order is (10 − 6)/2 = 2; the last two electrons are in the antibonding π* orbitals. Removing one electron to make O₂⁺ takes it from an antibonding orbital, giving (10 − 5)/2 = 2.5. Adding electrons puts them into antibonding orbitals: O₂⁻ has (10 − 7)/2 = 1.5 and O₂²⁻ has (10 − 8)/2 = 1. So the bond order is highest for O₂⁺, which also has the shortest and strongest bond.
Why not the others: (B) O₂ has bond order 2, less than 2.5. (C) O₂⁻ (superoxide) has one more antibonding electron than O₂, bond order 1.5. (D) O₂²⁻ (peroxide) has two more antibonding electrons, bond order 1, the lowest of the four.
Key point: Bond order = (bonding electrons − antibonding electrons)/2; for oxygen species, fewer π* electrons means a stronger bond.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: An aqueous Co(III) coordination salt has five NH₃, one Cl and one SO₄ per cobalt. The figure shows its two immediate ion tests. Which arrangement fits those results?
options: C) Both Cl and SO₄ are free counterions
D) Both Cl and SO₄ are coordinated ligands
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) [Co(NH₃)₅Cl]SO₄.
Why: Free sulfate precipitates as BaSO₄, while coordinated chloride does not supply immediate free Cl⁻ for AgCl. In (B), Co(III) plus one bound Cl⁻ gives the complex charge +2, balanced by one SO₄²⁻. The wet tests and electroneutrality agree; moving sulfate inside and chloride outside reverses the ionic responses.
Why not the others: (A) predicts AgCl instead of BaSO₄; (C) predicts both precipitates; (D) predicts neither.
Key point: Check free ions and complex charge together.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: For hydrogen, the longest-wavelength line in the Balmer series is at 656 nm. What is the wavelength of the Balmer series limit, approximately, using the Rydberg relation?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) About 365 nm.
Given: Longest Balmer wavelength (3 → 2) = 656 nm; the series limit is the transition ∞ → 2.
Formula/Principle: \(\dfrac1\lambda=R\left(\dfrac1{2^2}-\dfrac1{n^2}\right)\); wavelength is inversely proportional to the bracket.
Step 1: For 3 → 2: \(\tfrac14-\tfrac19=\tfrac5{36}\).
Step 2: For ∞ → 2: \(\tfrac14-0=\tfrac14=\tfrac9{36}\).
Step 3: \(\lambda_{\text{limit}}=656\times\dfrac{5/36}{9/36}\).
Worked derivation: \[\lambda_{\text{limit}}=656\times\frac59=364.4\ \mathrm{nm}\approx365\ \mathrm{nm}\]
Why: The longest wavelength in a series comes from the smallest energy jump, from the level just above. The series limit is the shortest wavelength, from an electron starting at n = ∞ (just free). Taking the ratio of the two cases cancels the Rydberg constant, so only the given wavelength is needed.
Why not the others: (A) 656 nm is the first line itself, not the limit. (B) 486 nm is the second Balmer line (4 → 2). (D) 1312 nm doubles the first wavelength; the limit must be shorter than every line in the series, not longer.
Key point: Series limit for final level n: \(\lambda=n^2/R\); for Balmer it is 4/R.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.topic: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: Which pair of compounds are metamers of each other?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Ethoxyethane and 1-methoxypropane.
Why: Metamers have the same molecular formula and the same functional group, but different alkyl groups on either side of that group. Ethoxyethane is C₂H₅–O–C₂H₅ and 1-methoxypropane is CH₃–O–C₃H₇. Both are ethers with formula C₄H₁₀O; only the split of the carbon atoms across the oxygen differs.
Why not the others: (A) Propan-1-ol and propan-2-ol differ in the position of the –OH group on the same chain, so they are position isomers. (B) Ethanol is an alcohol and methoxymethane is an ether, so they are functional isomers. (C) Butane and 2-methylpropane differ in the carbon skeleton, so they are chain isomers.
Key point: Metamerism: same functional group, different alkyl groups around it (common in ethers, ketones and secondary amines).

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Complete combustion of a 0.90 g compound containing only C, H and O gives 1.32 g CO₂ and 0.54 g H₂O. What is its empirical formula? Use C=12, H=1, O=16.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) CH₂O.
Given: Sample 0.90 g; \(\ce{CO2}\) 1.32 g; \(\ce{H2O}\) 0.54 g; C = 12, H = 1, O = 16.
Formula/Principle: All carbon ends up in \(\ce{CO2}\) and all hydrogen in \(\ce{H2O}\); oxygen is found by difference.
Step 1: \(n_C=1.32/44=0.030\ \mathrm{mol}\); mass of C \(=0.030\times12=0.36\ \mathrm g\).
Step 2: \(n_H=2\times(0.54/18)=0.060\ \mathrm{mol}\); mass of H \(=0.060\ \mathrm g\).
Step 3: Mass of O \(=0.90-0.36-0.06=0.48\ \mathrm g\); \(n_O=0.48/16=0.030\ \mathrm{mol}\).
Step 4: Divide by the smallest amount, 0.030.
Worked derivation: \[n_C:n_H:n_O=0.030:0.060:0.030=1:2:1\Rightarrow\ce{CH2O}\]
Why: Combustion turns each carbon atom into one \(\ce{CO2}\) and each pair of hydrogen atoms into one \(\ce{H2O}\). The oxygen in the products comes partly from the air, so the oxygen in the compound cannot be read from the products; it is the mass of the sample not accounted for by carbon and hydrogen.
Why not the others: (B) \(\ce{C2H6O}\) needs a C : H : O ratio of 2 : 6 : 1. (C) \(\ce{CH4O}\) has twice the hydrogen found. (D) \(\ce{C2H4O}\) has twice the carbon and hydrogen for the oxygen found.
Key point: Oxygen by difference; then divide every mole amount by the smallest.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Which reagents convert chlorobenzene directly into toluene?
options: B) CH₃Cl and sodium metal in dry ether
C) Aqueous KOH at room temperature
D) Magnesium in dry ether followed by water
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) CH₃Cl and sodium metal in dry ether.
Why: In the Wurtz–Fittig reaction an aryl halide and an alkyl halide are treated together with sodium in dry ether, and the aryl and alkyl groups join: \(\ce{C6H5Cl + CH3Cl + 2Na -> C6H5CH3 + 2NaCl}\). This replaces the chlorine on the ring by a methyl group in one step, giving toluene.
Why not the others: (A) CH₃Cl with anhydrous AlCl₃ is a Friedel–Crafts alkylation; it adds a methyl group to the ring but keeps the chlorine, giving chlorotoluenes. (C) Chlorobenzene does not react with aqueous KOH at room temperature, and even under drastic conditions the product would be phenol. (D) Magnesium gives phenylmagnesium chloride, which gives benzene with water, not toluene.
Key point: Wurtz: R–X + R–X; Fittig: Ar–X + Ar–X; Wurtz–Fittig: Ar–X + R–X, all with Na in dry ether.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Two colourless liquids each react with sodium metal to release H₂. Only liquid X also gives brisk CO₂ effervescence with aqueous NaHCO₃. Which assignment is consistent?
options: B) X is an alcohol; Y is a carboxylic acid
D) X is a carboxylic acid; Y can be an alcohol
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) X is a carboxylic acid; Y may be an alcohol.
Why: Sodium reacts with acidic O–H groups in both alcohols and carboxylic acids, so its positive test alone is not diagnostic. Bicarbonate is protonated by a carboxylic acid to yield carbonic acid and then CO₂; ordinary alcohols are too weakly acidic to give that reaction. The second reagent separates the possibilities.
Why not the others: (B) reverses the bicarbonate response; (C) phenols ordinarily do not liberate CO₂ from bicarbonate; (A) ethers lack the O–H group needed for the sodium test.
Key point: Use a discriminating second reagent after a non-specific first test.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: A sample gives both a silver mirror with Tollens reagent and a yellow precipitate in the iodoform test. Among these compounds, which fits both results?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Ethanal.
Why: Tollens reagent is reduced by the aldehyde group. The iodoform reaction requires a methyl carbonyl unit or a precursor oxidised to one; ethanal, \(\ce{CH3CHO}\), is the relevant aldehyde with this motif. Comparing the two tests excludes a methyl ketone that passes only the second and other aldehydes that lack the required methyl group.
Why not the others: (B) propanal lacks a methyl directly attached to the carbonyl; (C) propanone is a methyl ketone but normally fails Tollens; (D) benzaldehyde lacks the methyl-carbonyl unit.
Key point: Intersect the structural conditions of two wet tests.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: In water, p-methoxyaniline is more basic than p-nitroaniline. Which electronic comparison is most directly relevant, while keeping the same solvent and aniline framework?
options: A) Basicity is determined only by molecular mass
B) Nitro donates by resonance more strongly than methoxy
C) Both substituents remove the nitrogen lone pair
D) Methoxy donation favours nitrogen lone-pair availability relative to nitro withdrawal
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Para methoxy donation favours basicity over nitro withdrawal.
Why: The aniline nitrogen lone pair participates in conjugation with the ring. An electron-donating para substituent and a strongly withdrawing para nitro group shift the electron distribution in opposite directions; the latter reduces availability for protonation. Holding solvent and core structure fixed makes the comparison meaningful, although solvation also matters in absolute basicity.
Why not the others: (B) reverses substituent effects; (C) falsely removes a lone pair; (A) ignores proton affinity and solvation.
Key point: Compare substituent effects under the same solvent conditions.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: At the same temperature, equal-molality ideal solutions of glucose and fully dissociated CaCl₂ are prepared in the same solvent. What is the ratio of magnitudes of their freezing-point depressions, CaCl₂ to glucose?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 3:1.
Given: Equal molality m in the same solvent; glucose does not dissociate; \(\ce{CaCl2}\) dissociates completely.
Formula/Principle: \(\Delta T_f=iK_fm\).
Step 1: Glucose: \(i=1\).
Step 2: \(\ce{CaCl2 -> Ca^2+ + 2Cl-}\) gives three particles, so \(i=3\).
Worked derivation: \[\frac{\Delta T_f(\ce{CaCl2})}{\Delta T_f(\text{glucose})}=\frac{3K_fm}{1K_fm}=3\]
Why: Freezing-point depression is a colligative property, so it depends on how many dissolved particles there are, not on their kind. One formula unit of calcium chloride puts three ions into solution, so at the same molality it lowers the freezing point three times as much as glucose.
Why not the others: (A) 1 : 1 ignores dissociation. (B) 2 : 1 counts only the two chloride ions and leaves out the calcium ion. (D) 4 : 1 counts one particle too many.
Key point: For a fully dissociated salt, i = number of ions per formula unit.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: A weak-electrolyte solution is diluted tenfold. Its specific conductivity decreases, while its molar conductivity increases. Which explanation reconciles the trends?
options: A) Both ion concentration and dissociation per mole necessarily fall
B) Fewer ions per unit volume but greater dissociation per mole
C) The ions become chemically neutral on dilution
D) Specific and molar conductivity must always move together
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Ion density falls while degree of dissociation rises.
Why: Specific conductivity concerns conductance of a fixed geometry/volume, so dilution usually reduces charge carriers per unit volume. Molar conductivity scales conductance to one mole of electrolyte; increased dissociation of the weak electrolyte supplies more ions per initial formula unit, raising this quantity. The two measurements use different normalisations.
Why not the others: (A) predicts the wrong molar trend; (C) has no basis in simple dilution; (D) conflates volume and mole normalisation.
Key point: State what each conductivity is normalised to.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: The figure gives three initial-rate trials for A+B→products. From its controlled concentration changes, what is the overall reaction order?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Third order.
Given: From the figure, doubling [A] at fixed [B] raises the rate from 2 to 8 units; then doubling [B] at fixed [A] raises it from 8 to 16 units.
Formula/Principle: Rate \(=k[A]^m[B]^n\); doubling one concentration alone multiplies the rate by \(2^m\) or \(2^n\).
Step 1: \(2^m=8/2=4\), so \(m=2\).
Step 2: \(2^n=16/8=2\), so \(n=1\).
Worked derivation: \[m+n=2+1=3;\qquad\text{rate}=k[A]^2[B]\]
Why: Each pair of trials changes one concentration only, so the change in rate shows the order in that reactant. The overall order is the sum of the two exponents. It cannot be read from the equation A + B → products, which would wrongly suggest second order.
Why not the others: (A) 1 misses the squared dependence on A and the dependence on B. (B) 2 is the order in A alone, or the sum of the coefficients in the equation. (D) 4 would need the rate to rise fourfold when B is doubled.
Key point: Overall order = sum of the experimentally found exponents.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Relation between ΔH and ΔU for a gas-phase reaction
questions.question: For N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) → 2NH₃(g) at 300 K, what is ΔH − ΔU per mole of reaction as written? Treat the gases as ideal and take R=8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) −4.99 kJ.
Given: \(\ce{N2(g) + 3H2(g) -> 2NH3(g)}\); \(T=300\ \mathrm K\); \(R=8.314\ \mathrm{J\,K^{-1}mol^{-1}}\).
Formula/Principle: \(\Delta H=\Delta U+\Delta n_gRT\), where \(\Delta n_g\) = moles of gaseous products − moles of gaseous reactants.
Step 1: \(\Delta n_g=2-(1+3)=-2\).
Step 2: \(\Delta H-\Delta U=\Delta n_gRT=(-2)(8.314)(300)\ \mathrm J\).
Worked derivation: \[\Delta H-\Delta U=-2\times8.314\times300=-4988\ \mathrm J\approx-4.99\ \mathrm{kJ}\]
Why: Enthalpy includes the pressure–volume term: \(H=U+pV\). At constant pressure and temperature, the volume change comes from the change in the number of moles of gas. Here four moles of gas become two, so the surroundings do work on the system and ΔH is more negative than ΔU.
Why not the others: (A) +4.99 kJ has the sign of \(\Delta n_g\) reversed. (C) −2.49 kJ uses \(\Delta n_g=-1\). (D) 0 would be right only if the number of moles of gas did not change.
Key point: \(\Delta H=\Delta U+\Delta n_gRT\); count gaseous species only.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: A buffer contains 0.10 mol CH₃COOH and 0.10 mol CH₃COO⁻ in 1 L. After 0.02 mol strong acid is added with negligible volume change, what is the new pH? Use pKₐ=4.76 and log(2/3)=−0.176.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 4.58.
Given: 0.10 mol \(\ce{CH3COOH}\) and 0.10 mol \(\ce{CH3COO-}\) in 1 L; 0.02 mol strong acid added; \(pK_a=4.76\); \(\log(2/3)=-0.176\).
Formula/Principle: The added \(\ce{H+}\) reacts completely with acetate: \(\ce{CH3COO- + H+ -> CH3COOH}\). Then \(pH=pK_a+\log\dfrac{n_{\text{base}}}{n_{\text{acid}}}\).
Step 1: \(n_{\text{base}}=0.10-0.02=0.08\ \mathrm{mol}\).
Step 2: \(n_{\text{acid}}=0.10+0.02=0.12\ \mathrm{mol}\).
Step 3: Ratio \(=0.08/0.12=2/3\).
Worked derivation: \[pH=4.76+\log\frac23=4.76-0.176=4.58\]
Why: A buffer resists a change in pH because its base component removes added acid. The strong acid is used up, turning some acetate into acetic acid, so the ratio of base to acid falls from 1 to 2/3 and the pH drops only slightly. The volume is the same for both species, so moles can be used in place of concentrations.
Why not the others: (B) 4.76 is the pH before the acid was added, when the ratio was 1. (C) 4.94 uses the ratio upside down (3/2), as if a base had been added. (D) 5.11 is higher than the starting pH, which cannot happen on adding acid.
Key point: Do the neutralisation in moles first, then apply the Henderson equation.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Which of the following ions is colourless in aqueous solution? (Atomic numbers: Ti 22, Fe 26, Cu 29, Zn 30.)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Zn²⁺.
Why: The colour of transition-metal ions in water comes from d–d transitions, which need a partly filled d subshell. Zn (Z = 30) is 3d¹⁰4s², so Zn²⁺ is 3d¹⁰. Its d subshell is full, no d–d transition is possible, and the ion is colourless.
Why not the others: (A) Cu²⁺ is 3d⁹, with one vacancy in the d subshell; its aqueous solution is blue. (B) Fe³⁺ is 3d⁵, partly filled; its aqueous solution is yellow. (C) Ti³⁺ is 3d¹, with one d electron that can be excited; its aqueous solution is purple.
Key point: d⁰ and d¹⁰ ions (Sc³⁺, Ti⁴⁺, Zn²⁺, Cu⁺) are colourless.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: A circle \(x^2+y^2-6x+2y-6=0\) is cut by the line \(y=1\). If the line is shifted upward by 2 units, by how much does the length of its chord decrease?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(4\sqrt{3}\).
Given: \(x^2+y^2-6x+2y-6=0;\quad\text{lines }y=1\ \text{and}\ y=3\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{chord}=2\sqrt{r^2-d^2}\)
Step 1: \((x-3)^2+(y+1)^2=16\Rightarrow\text{centre }(3,-1),\ r=4\)
Step 2: \(y=1:\ d=|1-(-1)|=2,\quad\ell_1=2\sqrt{16-4}=4\sqrt3\)
Step 3: \(y=3:\ d=|3-(-1)|=4=r,\quad\ell_2=2\sqrt{16-16}=0\)
Worked derivation: \[\ell_1-\ell_2=4\sqrt3-0=4\sqrt3\]
Check: \[y=1:\ (x-3)^2=12\Rightarrow x=3\pm2\sqrt3;\qquad y=3:\ (x-3)^2=0\ (\text{tangent})\]
Why: \(d=r\Rightarrow\text{tangent}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(2r=8\) (diameter); (B) \(2\sqrt{16-1}=2\sqrt{15}\) (\(d=1\)); (C) \(\sqrt{16-4}=2\sqrt3\) (half-chord).
Key point: \(\left(\dfrac{\ell}{2}\right)^2+d^2=r^2\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: Let \(f(x)=x^2\sin(1/x)\) for \(x\ne0\), and \(f(0)=0\). For which real k is \(g(x)=f(x)+k|x|\) differentiable at zero?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Only \(k=0\).
Given: \(f(x)=x^2\sin\dfrac1x\ (x\ne0),\ f(0)=0;\quad g(x)=f(x)+k|x|\)
Formula/Principle: \(g'(0)=\displaystyle\lim_{h\to0}\frac{g(h)-g(0)}{h}\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac{f(h)}{h}=h\sin\dfrac1h,\quad\left|h\sin\dfrac1h\right|\le|h|\to0\)
Step 2: \(\dfrac{k|h|}{h}=+k\ (h>0),\quad-k\ (h<0)\)
Step 3: \(g'(0^+)=k,\quad g'(0^-)=-k\)
Worked derivation: \[g'(0^+)=g'(0^-)\iff k=-k\iff k=0\]
Check: \[k=0:\ g=f,\ g'(0)=0\]
Why: \(-|h|\le h\sin\dfrac1h\le|h|\)
Why not the others: (A) \(k=1:\ g'(0^+)=1\ne-1=g'(0^-)\); (B) \(k=1:\ 1\ne-1\); (D) \(k=0:\ g'(0)=0\ \text{exists}\).
Key point: \(|x|\ \text{is not differentiable at }0\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: Find the maximum of \(f(x)=x^3-3x\) on the closed interval \([-2,1]\).
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 2.
Given: \(f(x)=x^3-3x,\quad x\in[-2,1]\)
Formula/Principle: \(\max_{[a,b]}f=\max\{f(a),\ f(b),\ f(c):\ f'(c)=0\}\)
Step 1: \(f'(x)=3x^2-3=0\Rightarrow x=\pm1\)
Step 2: \(f(-2)=-8+6=-2\)
Step 3: \(f(-1)=-1+3=2\)
Step 4: \(f(1)=1-3=-2\)
Worked derivation: \[\max\{-2,\ 2,\ -2\}=2\ \ \text{at }x=-1\]
Check: \[f''(-1)=-6<0\ (\text{local maximum})\]
Why: \(f\ \text{continuous on a closed interval}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(f(0)=0<2\); (C) \(-2=f(-2)=f(1)\ (\text{minimum})\); (D) \(f(x)\le2<3\ \text{on }[-2,1]\).
Key point: \(\text{compare critical values with endpoint values}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: Evaluate \(I=\int_{-1}^{1}\left(\frac{x^3+2x}{1+x^2}+\frac{2}{1+x^2}\right)dx\).
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(\pi\).
Given: \(I=\displaystyle\int_{-1}^{1}\left(\frac{x^3+2x}{1+x^2}+\frac{2}{1+x^2}\right)dx\)
Formula/Principle: \(\displaystyle\int_{-a}^{a}h(x)\,dx=0\ (h\ \text{odd}),\quad=2\int_0^ah(x)\,dx\ (h\ \text{even})\)
Step 1: \(h_1(x)=\dfrac{x^3+2x}{1+x^2}:\ h_1(-x)=-h_1(x)\Rightarrow\displaystyle\int_{-1}^{1}h_1\,dx=0\)
Step 2: \(\displaystyle\int_{-1}^{1}\frac{2}{1+x^2}dx=2\left[\tan^{-1}x\right]_{-1}^{1}=2\left(\frac\pi4+\frac\pi4\right)\)
Worked derivation: \[I=0+\pi=\pi\]
Check: \[\frac{x^3+2x}{1+x^2}=x+\frac{x}{1+x^2}\ \ (\text{sum of odd functions})\]
Why: \(\text{interval symmetric about }0\)
Why not the others: (A) \(0\) (even term omitted); (C) \(\dfrac\pi2=\displaystyle\int_{-1}^{1}\frac{dx}{1+x^2}\) (factor 2 omitted); (D) \(2\pi\) (\(\tan^{-1}1=\tfrac\pi2\)).
Key point: \(\text{split the integrand into odd and even parts}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: On the domain [1,∞), let f(x)=x+1/x. Which formula gives its inverse, including the correct domain of the inverse?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \((y+\sqrt{y^2-4})/2\), y≥2.
Given: \(f(x)=x+\dfrac1x,\quad x\ge1\)
Formula/Principle: \(y=f(x)\Rightarrow x^2-yx+1=0\)
Step 1: \(f'(x)=1-\dfrac{1}{x^2}\ge0\ (x\ge1),\quad f(1)=2\Rightarrow\text{range }[2,\infty)\)
Step 2: \(x=\dfrac{y\pm\sqrt{y^2-4}}{2}\)
Step 3: \(x_+x_-=1,\ x_+\ge x_-\Rightarrow x_+\ge1\ge x_-\)
Worked derivation: \[f^{-1}(y)=\frac{y+\sqrt{y^2-4}}{2},\quad y\ge2\]
Check: \[y=\tfrac52:\ \frac{2.5+\sqrt{2.25}}{2}=2,\qquad f(2)=2+\tfrac12=\tfrac52\]
Why: \(x\ge1\ \text{selects the larger root}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(y=\tfrac52:\ \dfrac{2.5-1.5}{2}=\tfrac12<1\); (C) \(\sqrt{y^2+4}\ \text{solves}\ x-\dfrac1x=y\); (D) \(y=\tfrac52:\ y-\dfrac1y=2.1,\ f(2.1)\approx2.58\ne2.5\).
Key point: \(\text{choose the root that lies in the stated domain}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: Vectors \(\mathbf a=(1,2,0)\), \(\mathbf b=(0,1,1)\) and \(\mathbf c=(t,0,1)\) are coplanar for what value of t?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(t=-1/2\).
Given: \(\mathbf a=(1,2,0),\quad\mathbf b=(0,1,1),\quad\mathbf c=(t,0,1)\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{coplanar}\iff\mathbf a\cdot(\mathbf b\times\mathbf c)=0\)
Step 1: \(\mathbf b\times\mathbf c=(1\cdot1-1\cdot0,\ 1\cdot t-0\cdot1,\ 0\cdot0-1\cdot t)=(1,\ t,\ -t)\)
Step 2: \(\mathbf a\cdot(\mathbf b\times\mathbf c)=1+2t+0=1+2t\)
Worked derivation: \[1+2t=0\Rightarrow t=-\frac12\]
Check: \[\begin{vmatrix}1&2&0\\0&1&1\\-\tfrac12&0&1\end{vmatrix}=1(1)-2\left(0+\tfrac12\right)+0=0\]
Why: \(\text{volume of the parallelepiped}=0\)
Why not the others: (A) \(t=-2:\ 1+2t=-3\ne0\); (B) \(t=2:\ 5\ne0\); (C) \(t=1:\ 3\ne0\).
Key point: \([\mathbf a\ \mathbf b\ \mathbf c]=0\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Singular matrix and a nonzero solution of Av = 0
questions.question: For which real a is \(A=\begin{pmatrix}1&a&0\\0&1&a\\a&0&1\end{pmatrix}\) singular, and which nonzero vector v satisfies Av=0 at that value?
options: D) A is nonsingular for every real a
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) a=−1; v=(1,1,1).
Given: \(A=\begin{pmatrix}1&a&0\\0&1&a\\a&0&1\end{pmatrix}\)
Formula/Principle: \(A\ \text{singular}\iff\det A=0\)
Step 1: \(\det A=1(1\cdot1-a\cdot0)-a(0\cdot1-a\cdot a)+0=1+a^3\)
Step 2: \(1+a^3=(a+1)(a^2-a+1)=0,\quad a^2-a+1=\left(a-\tfrac12\right)^2+\tfrac34>0\Rightarrow a=-1\)
Step 3: \(a=-1:\ x-y=0,\quad y-z=0,\quad-x+z=0\Rightarrow x=y=z\)
Worked derivation: \[a=-1,\qquad\mathbf v=(1,1,1)\]
Check: \[\begin{pmatrix}1&-1&0\\0&1&-1\\-1&0&1\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\\1\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}0\\0\\0\end{pmatrix}\]
Why: \(A\mathbf v=\mathbf 0,\ \mathbf v\ne\mathbf 0\iff\det A=0\)
Why not the others: (B) \((1,-1,1):\ x-y=2\ne0\); (C) \(a=1:\ \det A=2\ne0\); (D) \(\det A=0\ \text{at }a=-1\).
Key point: \(a^3+1=(a+1)(a^2-a+1)\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Conditional probability with two dice rolls
questions.question: A fair die is rolled twice. Given that the first roll shows an even number, what is the probability that the sum of the two rolls is 8?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 1/6.
Given: \(\text{two rolls }(d_1,d_2);\quad E:\ d_1\in\{2,4,6\};\quad S:\ d_1+d_2=8\)
Formula/Principle: \(P(S|E)=\dfrac{n(S\cap E)}{n(E)}\)
Step 1: \(n(E)=3\times6=18\)
Step 2: \(S\cap E=\{(2,6),\ (4,4),\ (6,2)\}\Rightarrow3\)
Worked derivation: \[P(S|E)=\frac{3}{18}=\frac16\]
Check: \[\text{each even }d_1\ \text{has exactly one }d_2=8-d_1\in\{1,\dots,6\}\Rightarrow\frac16\]
Why: \(d_2=8-d_1:\ 6,\ 4,\ 2\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\dfrac{5}{36}=P(S)\) (condition ignored); (B) \(\dfrac{4}{36}=\dfrac19\); (D) \(\dfrac{6}{18}=\dfrac13\).
Key point: \(\text{restrict the sample space to the given event}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Committee selection with an 'at least' condition
questions.question: A committee of 5 is to be chosen from 6 men and 4 women. How many committees contain at least 3 women?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 66.
Given: \(6\ \text{men},\ 4\ \text{women};\quad5\ \text{chosen},\ \text{women}\ge3\)
Formula/Principle: \(N=\dbinom43\dbinom62+\dbinom44\dbinom61\)
Step 1: \(3\ \text{women},\ 2\ \text{men}:\ \dbinom43\dbinom62=4\times15=60\)
Step 2: \(4\ \text{women},\ 1\ \text{man}:\ \dbinom44\dbinom61=1\times6=6\)
Worked derivation: \[N=60+6=66\]
Check: \[\binom{10}{5}=252=\underbrace{6}_{0W}+\underbrace{60}_{1W}+\underbrace{120}_{2W}+\underbrace{60}_{3W}+\underbrace{6}_{4W}\]
Why: \(\text{cases with different numbers of women are disjoint}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(60\) (4 women omitted); (C) \(120+60+6=186\) (women \(\ge2\)); (D) \(252-6=246\) (women \(\ge1\)).
Key point: \(\text{'at least' = sum over the allowed cases}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: What is the coefficient of \(x^4\) in \((1-x)^5(1+x)^4\)?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 6.
Given: \((1-x)^5(1+x)^4\)
Formula/Principle: \((1-x)(1+x)=1-x^2\)
Step 1: \((1-x)^5(1+x)^4=(1-x)\left(1-x^2\right)^4\)
Step 2: \(\left(1-x^2\right)^4=1-4x^2+6x^4-4x^6+x^8\)
Step 3: \([x^4]=1\times6+(-1)\times[x^3]\left(1-x^2\right)^4=6+0\)
Worked derivation: \[[x^4]=6\]
Check: \[\sum_{k}\binom5k(-1)^k\binom4{4-k}=1-20+60-40+5=6\]
Why: \(\left(1-x^2\right)^4\ \text{has even powers only}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(-6\) (sign of \(\binom42(-1)^2\)); (B) \(-1\); (C) \(+1=[x^0]\).
Key point: \((1-x)^{m+1}(1+x)^m=(1-x)(1-x^2)^m\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Equal-length GP blocks and an infinite geometric sum
questions.question: A decreasing geometric progression has positive first term. The sum of its first three terms is 7, and the sum of its next three terms is 7/8. What is the sum to infinity?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 8.
Given: \(a>0,\ 0<r<1;\quad a+ar+ar^2=7;\quad ar^3+ar^4+ar^5=\dfrac78\)
Formula/Principle: \(ar^3+ar^4+ar^5=r^3(a+ar+ar^2);\quad S_\infty=\dfrac{a}{1-r}\)
Step 1: \(r^3=\dfrac{7/8}{7}=\dfrac18\Rightarrow r=\dfrac12\)
Step 2: \(a\left(1+\tfrac12+\tfrac14\right)=7\Rightarrow\tfrac74a=7\Rightarrow a=4\)
Worked derivation: \[S_\infty=\frac{4}{1-\frac12}=8\]
Check: \[4+2+1=7;\qquad\tfrac12+\tfrac14+\tfrac18=\tfrac78\]
Why: \(|r|<1\Rightarrow S_\infty\ \text{exists}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(7=S_3\); (C) \(\dfrac{7}{1-\frac12}=14\) (\(a=7\)); (D) \(\dfrac{4}{1-\frac12}\times2=16\).
Key point: \(S_\infty=\dfrac{S_3}{1-r^3}=\dfrac{7}{7/8}=8\)
questions.syllabus_anchor: Sequences and series: finite and infinite geometric sums

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: The quadratics \(x^2-3x+2\) and \(x^2-(a+1)x+a^2-1\) share at least one real root. What is the sum of all distinct real values of a that allow this?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 2.
Given: \(p(x)=x^2-3x+2=(x-1)(x-2);\quad q(x)=x^2-(a+1)x+a^2-1\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{common root}\Rightarrow q(1)=0\ \text{or}\ q(2)=0\)
Step 1: \(q(1)=1-(a+1)+a^2-1=a^2-a-1=0\Rightarrow a=\dfrac{1\pm\sqrt5}{2}\)
Step 2: \(q(2)=4-2(a+1)+a^2-1=a^2-2a+1=0\Rightarrow a=1\)
Step 3: \(\dfrac{1+\sqrt5}{2}+\dfrac{1-\sqrt5}{2}=1\)
Worked derivation: \[\sum a=1+1=2\]
Check: \[a=1:\ q=x^2-2x=x(x-2),\ \text{common root }2\]
Why: \(\text{three distinct values: }\dfrac{1+\sqrt5}{2},\ \dfrac{1-\sqrt5}{2},\ 1\)
Why not the others: (A) \(1\) (only the pair from \(q(1)=0\), or only \(a=1\)); (B) \(3\) (\(a=1\) counted twice); (D) \(\dfrac{1+\sqrt5}{2}\) (one value only).
Key point: \(\text{test every root of the factorised quadratic}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: A dataset has mean 5 and standard deviation 3. Each observation becomes \(y=2x+c\), and the new mean is 17. What is the new standard deviation?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 6.
Given: \(\bar x=5,\ \sigma_x=3;\quad y=2x+c;\quad\bar y=17\)
Formula/Principle: \(\bar y=2\bar x+c,\quad\sigma_y=|2|\,\sigma_x\)
Step 1: \(17=10+c\Rightarrow c=7\)
Worked derivation: \[\sigma_y=2\times3=6\]
Check: \[y-\bar y=2(x-\bar x)\Rightarrow\sigma_y^2=4\sigma_x^2=36\]
Why: \(\text{adding }c\ \text{shifts every value equally}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(3=\sigma_x\) (scale ignored); (B) \(9=\sigma_x^2\); (D) \(4\times3=12\) (variance factor applied to \(\sigma\)).
Key point: \(\sigma_{ax+b}=|a|\,\sigma_x\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: A positive solution satisfies \(dy/dx=xy^2\), y(0)=1. At which positive x does it first reach y=2?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) x=1.
Given: \(\dfrac{dy}{dx}=xy^2,\quad y(0)=1,\quad y>0\)
Formula/Principle: \(\displaystyle\int\frac{dy}{y^2}=\int x\,dx\)
Step 1: \(-\dfrac1y=\dfrac{x^2}{2}+C\)
Step 2: \(y(0)=1:\ -1=C\)
Step 3: \(y=\dfrac{1}{1-\frac{x^2}{2}}\)
Worked derivation: \[y=2:\ 1-\frac{x^2}{2}=\frac12\Rightarrow x^2=1\Rightarrow x=1\]
Check: \[y'=\frac{x}{\left(1-\frac{x^2}{2}\right)^2}=xy^2\]
Why: \(y\ \text{increases for }0<x<\sqrt2\)
Why not the others: (A) \(x=\tfrac12:\ y=\dfrac{1}{1-\frac18}=\dfrac87\); (B) \(x=2>\sqrt2:\ y<0\); (C) \(x=\sqrt2:\ y\to\infty\).
Key point: \(\text{separate, integrate, then apply the initial condition}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: For \(f(x)=|x-1|/(x^2-1)\), x≠1, what are its left and right limits at x=1, in order?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (−1/2,1/2).
Given: \(f(x)=\dfrac{|x-1|}{x^2-1},\quad x\ne1\)
Formula/Principle: \(|x-1|=-(x-1)\ (x<1),\quad|x-1|=x-1\ (x>1)\)
Step 1: \(x<1:\ f=\dfrac{-(x-1)}{(x-1)(x+1)}=-\dfrac{1}{x+1}\)
Step 2: \(x>1:\ f=\dfrac{x-1}{(x-1)(x+1)}=\dfrac{1}{x+1}\)
Worked derivation: \[\lim_{x\to1^-}f=-\frac12,\qquad\lim_{x\to1^+}f=+\frac12\]
Check: \[f(0.9)=\frac{0.1}{-0.19}\approx-0.53;\qquad f(1.1)=\frac{0.1}{0.21}\approx0.48\]
Why: \(x^2-1=(x-1)(x+1)\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\left(\tfrac12,\tfrac12\right)\) (\(|x-1|=x-1\) on both sides); (C) \(\left(\tfrac12,-\tfrac12\right)\) (order reversed); (D) \(\left(-\tfrac12,-\tfrac12\right)\) (\(|x-1|=1-x\) on both sides).
Key point: \(\dfrac{|x-a|}{x-a}=\pm1\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Dimensional analysis of an oscillation period
questions.question: The period T of small oscillations of a liquid drop depends only on its density ρ, its radius r and the surface tension S, as T ∝ ρᵃ rᵇ Sᶜ. What are (a, b, c)?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (1/2, 3/2, −1/2).
Given: \(T\propto\rho^ar^bS^c\)
Formula/Principle: \([T]=[\rho]^a[r]^b[S]^c;\quad[\rho]=ML^{-3},\ [r]=L,\ [S]=\dfrac{[F]}{[L]}=MT^{-2}\)
Step 1: \(M^0L^0T^1=M^{a+c}L^{-3a+b}T^{-2c}\)
Step 2: \(T:\ -2c=1\Rightarrow c=-\tfrac12\)
Step 3: \(M:\ a+c=0\Rightarrow a=\tfrac12\)
Step 4: \(L:\ -3a+b=0\Rightarrow b=\tfrac32\)
Worked derivation: \[T\propto\sqrt{\frac{\rho r^3}{S}}\]
Check: \[\left[\frac{\rho r^3}{S}\right]=\frac{(ML^{-3})(L^3)}{MT^{-2}}=T^2\]
Why: \(\text{both sides must have the same dimensions}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(b=\tfrac12:\ L^{-3/2+1/2}=L^{-1}\ne L^0\); (B) \(c=+\tfrac12:\ T^{-1}\ne T^{1}\); (D) \((1,3,-1):\ T^{2}\ne T^{1}\).
Key point: \(\text{equate the powers of }M,\ L,\ T\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Block sliding down a rough incline
questions.question: A block slides down a rough plane inclined at 37° to the horizontal. The coefficient of kinetic friction is 0.5. Taking g=10 m s⁻², sin 37°=0.6 and cos 37°=0.8, what is the acceleration of the block?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 2 m s⁻².
Given: \(\theta=37^\circ,\quad\mu_k=0.5,\quad g=10\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}},\quad\sin37^\circ=0.6,\ \cos37^\circ=0.8\)
Formula/Principle: \(N=mg\cos\theta,\quad ma=mg\sin\theta-\mu_kN\)
Step 1: \(a=g(\sin\theta-\mu_k\cos\theta)\)
Step 2: \(a=10\,(0.6-0.5\times0.8)\)
Worked derivation: \[a=10\,(0.6-0.4)=2\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\]
Check: \[\tan37^\circ=0.75>\mu_k=0.5\Rightarrow\text{block slides}\]
Why: \(f_k=\mu_kN\ \text{up the incline}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(g\sin\theta=6\) (friction omitted); (B) \(g=10\) (free fall); (D) \(\mu_kg\cos\theta=4\) (friction term only).
Key point: \(a=g(\sin\theta-\mu_k\cos\theta)\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: A wire within its elastic limit has length L, area A and strain ε. If L and A are both doubled while ε is kept unchanged, by what factor does stored elastic energy change?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Factor 4.
Given: \(L\to2L,\quad A\to2A,\quad\varepsilon\ \text{unchanged},\quad Y\ \text{same}\)
Formula/Principle: \(U=\tfrac12\times\text{stress}\times\text{strain}\times\text{volume}=\tfrac12Y\varepsilon^2AL\)
Step 1: \(U'=\tfrac12Y\varepsilon^2(2A)(2L)\)
Worked derivation: \[\frac{U'}{U}=\frac{(2A)(2L)}{AL}=4\]
Check: \[u=\tfrac12Y\varepsilon^2\ \text{unchanged};\quad V'=4V\]
Why: \(U=u\times V\)
Why not the others: (A) \(1\) (energy density only); (B) \(2\) (only \(L\) or only \(A\) doubled); (C) \(8\).
Key point: \(U=\tfrac12Y\varepsilon^2\,AL\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: Two slabs of the same cross-section are in steady series heat flow. Slab 1 has thickness 2d and conductivity 2k; slab 2 thickness d and conductivity k. What fraction of the total temperature drop is across slab 1?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 1/2.
Given: \(\text{slab 1: }2d,\ 2k;\quad\text{slab 2: }d,\ k;\quad\text{same }A;\quad\text{series, steady}\)
Formula/Principle: \(R_{th}=\dfrac{L}{kA},\quad\Delta T_i=HR_i\)
Step 1: \(R_1=\dfrac{2d}{2kA}=\dfrac{d}{kA}\)
Step 2: \(R_2=\dfrac{d}{kA}\)
Worked derivation: \[\frac{\Delta T_1}{\Delta T}=\frac{R_1}{R_1+R_2}=\frac12\]
Check: \[H=\frac{2kA\,\Delta T_1}{2d}=\frac{kA\,\Delta T_2}{d}\Rightarrow\Delta T_1=\Delta T_2\]
Why: \(\text{steady state}\Rightarrow\text{same }H\ \text{through both slabs}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\dfrac14\); (C) \(\dfrac{2d}{2d+d}=\dfrac23\) (thickness only); (D) \(\dfrac34\).
Key point: \(\Delta T_i\propto\dfrac{L_i}{k_i}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: At fixed temperature, a dilute ideal gas's pressure doubles while molecular collision diameter is unchanged. How do mean free path and mean molecular speed change?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Path halves; speed unchanged.
Given: \(T\ \text{fixed},\quad P\to2P,\quad d\ \text{fixed}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\lambda=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2\,\pi d^2n},\quad n=\dfrac{P}{k_BT},\quad\bar v=\sqrt{\dfrac{8k_BT}{\pi m}}\)
Step 1: \(n\to2n\)
Step 2: \(\lambda=\dfrac{k_BT}{\sqrt2\,\pi d^2P}\to\dfrac\lambda2\)
Worked derivation: \[\lambda'=\frac\lambda2,\qquad\bar v'=\bar v\]
Check: \[\text{collision frequency}=\frac{\bar v}{\lambda}\to2\,\frac{\bar v}{\lambda}\]
Why: \(\bar v\ \text{depends only on }T\ \text{and}\ m\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\lambda\propto\dfrac1P,\ \bar v\ \text{fixed}\); (B) \(\bar v\ \text{fixed at constant }T\); (C) \(\lambda\ \text{changes with }n\).
Key point: \(\lambda\propto\dfrac TP\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Speed at a given displacement in simple harmonic motion
questions.question: A particle performs simple harmonic motion with amplitude 5 cm and angular frequency 4 rad s⁻¹. What is its speed when it is 3 cm from the mean position?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 16 cm s⁻¹.
Given: \(A=5\ \mathrm{cm},\quad\omega=4\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}},\quad x=3\ \mathrm{cm}\)
Formula/Principle: \(v=\omega\sqrt{A^2-x^2}\)
Step 1: \(A^2-x^2=25-9=16\ \mathrm{cm^2}\)
Worked derivation: \[v=4\times\sqrt{16}=16\ \mathrm{cm\,s^{-1}}\]
Check: \[v_{\max}=\omega A=20\ \mathrm{cm\,s^{-1}};\quad\left(\frac{16}{20}\right)^2+\left(\frac35\right)^2=0.64+0.36=1\]
Why: \(\tfrac12mv^2+\tfrac12m\omega^2x^2=\tfrac12m\omega^2A^2\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\omega x=12\); (C) \(\omega A=20=v_{\max}\); (D) \(\omega(A-x)=8\).
Key point: \(v^2=\omega^2(A^2-x^2)\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: A string pulse reflects inverted from a junction with a much heavier string. What boundary behaviour explains the inversion?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Approximately fixed end.
Given: \(\mu_2\gg\mu_1\ \ (\text{same tension})\)
Formula/Principle: \(v=\sqrt{\dfrac T\mu};\quad\text{fixed end: }y(\text{junction},t)=0\Rightarrow y_r=-y_i\)
Step 1: \(\mu_2\gg\mu_1\Rightarrow\text{junction displacement}\approx0\)
Step 2: \(y_i+y_r=0\ \text{at the junction}\)
Worked derivation: \[y_r=-y_i\quad(\text{phase change of }\pi)\]
Check: \[\mu_2\ll\mu_1\ (\text{free end}):\ y_r=+y_i\]
Why: \(\text{a much heavier string hardly moves}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\text{free end}\Rightarrow y_r=+y_i\); (C) \(f_r=f_i>0\); (D) \(v_r=v_i=\sqrt{T/\mu_1}\).
Key point: \(\text{rigid boundary: inverted reflection};\ \text{free boundary: upright reflection}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Electric Charges and Fields / Electrostatic Potential
questions.question: The figure marks +q at x=0 and +4q at x=3a. Where between them is the net electric field zero?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) x=a.
Given: \(+q\ \text{at }x=0,\quad+4q\ \text{at }x=3a,\quad0<x<3a\)
Formula/Principle: \(E=\dfrac{kq}{r^2};\quad E_{\text{net}}=0\iff\dfrac{kq}{x^2}=\dfrac{4kq}{(3a-x)^2}\)
Step 1: \((3a-x)^2=4x^2\)
Step 2: \(3a-x=2x\ \ (x>0,\ 3a-x>0)\)
Worked derivation: \[x=a\]
Check: \[x=a:\ \frac{kq}{a^2}=\frac{4kq}{(2a)^2}\]
Why: \(\text{between like charges the two fields point in opposite directions}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\dfrac{kq}{a^2}=\dfrac{4kq}{4a^2}\ \text{at }x=a\); (B) \(x=\tfrac32a:\ \dfrac{kq}{2.25a^2}\ne\dfrac{4kq}{2.25a^2}\); (C) \(x=2a:\ \dfrac{kq}{4a^2}\ne\dfrac{4kq}{a^2}\).
Key point: \(\dfrac{r_1}{r_2}=\sqrt{\dfrac{q_1}{q_2}}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Maximum power delivered by a cell with internal resistance
questions.question: A battery of emf 12 V and internal resistance 2 Ω is connected to a variable resistor R. For which value of R is the power dissipated in R the greatest, and what is that power?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 2 Ω; 18 W.
Given: \(\mathcal E=12\ \mathrm V,\quad r=2\ \Omega\)
Formula/Principle: \(P=I^2R=\dfrac{\mathcal E^2R}{(R+r)^2}\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac{dP}{dR}=\mathcal E^2\,\dfrac{(R+r)^2-2R(R+r)}{(R+r)^4}=\mathcal E^2\,\dfrac{r-R}{(R+r)^3}\)
Step 2: \(\dfrac{dP}{dR}=0\Rightarrow R=r=2\ \Omega\)
Step 3: \(I=\dfrac{12}{2+2}=3\ \mathrm A\)
Worked derivation: \[P_{\max}=I^2R=3^2\times2=18\ \mathrm W=\frac{\mathcal E^2}{4r}\]
Check: \[R=1\ \Omega:\ I=4\ \mathrm A,\ P=16\ \mathrm W;\qquad R=4\ \Omega:\ I=2\ \mathrm A,\ P=16\ \mathrm W\]
Why: \(\dfrac{dP}{dR}>0\ (R<r),\quad\dfrac{dP}{dR}<0\ (R>r)\)
Why not the others: (A) \(R=1\ \Omega:\ 16\ \mathrm W<18\ \mathrm W\); (B) \(R=4\ \Omega:\ 16\ \mathrm W<18\ \mathrm W\); (D) \(\mathcal EI=12\times3=36\ \mathrm W\) (total power of the cell).
Key point: \(P_{\max}=\dfrac{\mathcal E^2}{4r}\ \text{at }R=r\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: A conducting rod rotates about one end at angular speed ω in perpendicular uniform field B. If only its outer half, r∈[L/2,L], is conducting, what fraction of full-rod emf is across that segment?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 3/4.
Given: \(\text{rod }0\le r\le L,\ \omega,\ B\perp\text{plane};\quad\text{segment }\tfrac L2\le r\le L\)
Formula/Principle: \(d\mathcal E=B\,v\,dr=B\omega r\,dr\)
Step 1: \(\mathcal E_{\text{full}}=\displaystyle\int_0^LB\omega r\,dr=\tfrac12B\omega L^2\)
Step 2: \(\mathcal E_{\text{outer}}=\displaystyle\int_{L/2}^{L}B\omega r\,dr=\tfrac12B\omega\left(L^2-\tfrac{L^2}{4}\right)=\tfrac38B\omega L^2\)
Worked derivation: \[\frac{\mathcal E_{\text{outer}}}{\mathcal E_{\text{full}}}=\frac{3/8}{1/2}=\frac34\]
Check: \[\mathcal E_{\text{inner}}=\tfrac12B\omega\left(\tfrac L2\right)^2=\tfrac18B\omega L^2,\qquad\tfrac18+\tfrac38=\tfrac12\]
Why: \(v=\omega r\ \text{increases with }r\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\dfrac14=\dfrac{\mathcal E_{\text{inner}}}{\mathcal E_{\text{full}}}\); (B) \(\dfrac12\) (length fraction); (D) \(\mathcal E_{\text{inner}}\ne0\).
Key point: \(\mathcal E=\tfrac12B\omega\left(r_2^2-r_1^2\right)\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: A series AC circuit has R=30 Ω, XL=40 Ω and XC=30 Ω. With 100 V rms supply, what is rms current?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) √10 A.
Given: \(R=30\ \Omega,\quad X_L=40\ \Omega,\quad X_C=30\ \Omega,\quad V=100\ \mathrm V\)
Formula/Principle: \(Z=\sqrt{R^2+(X_L-X_C)^2},\quad I=\dfrac VZ\)
Step 1: \(X_L-X_C=10\ \Omega\)
Step 2: \(Z=\sqrt{900+100}=10\sqrt{10}\ \Omega\)
Worked derivation: \[I=\frac{100}{10\sqrt{10}}=\frac{10}{\sqrt{10}}=\sqrt{10}\ \mathrm A\approx3.16\ \mathrm A\]
Check: \[V_R=30\sqrt{10},\ V_L-V_C=10\sqrt{10}:\ \sqrt{9000+1000}=100\ \mathrm V\]
Why: \(V_L\ \text{and}\ V_C\ \text{are in antiphase}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(Z=\sqrt{30^2+40^2}=50\ \Omega\Rightarrow2\ \mathrm A\) (\(X_C\) omitted); (C) \(Z=R=30\ \Omega\Rightarrow\tfrac{10}{3}\ \mathrm A\) (reactance omitted); (D) \(Z=30-10=20\ \Omega\Rightarrow5\ \mathrm A\) (scalar subtraction).
Key point: \(Z=\sqrt{R^2+(X_L-X_C)^2}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: A converging lens produces an upright virtual image of an object inside its focal length. In the Cartesian convention with incident light left-to-right, what signs have image distance v and magnification m?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) v<0, m>0.
Given: \(\text{converging lens},\ f>0;\quad u=-|u|,\ |u|<f\)
Formula/Principle: \(\dfrac1v-\dfrac1u=\dfrac1f,\quad m=\dfrac vu\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac1v=\dfrac1f+\dfrac1u=\dfrac1f-\dfrac{1}{|u|}\)
Step 2: \(|u|<f\Rightarrow\dfrac1v<0\Rightarrow v<0\)
Worked derivation: \[m=\frac vu=\frac{(-)}{(-)}>0\]
Check: \[f=10,\ u=-5:\ \frac1v=\frac1{10}-\frac15=-\frac1{10},\ v=-10\ \mathrm{cm},\ m=+2\]
Why: \(v<0\Rightarrow\text{image on the object side (virtual)};\ m>0\Rightarrow\text{upright}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\dfrac1v\ne\infty\); (B) \(v>0\Rightarrow\text{real image}\); (C) \(m<0\Rightarrow\text{inverted}\).
Key point: \(|u|<f\Rightarrow\text{virtual, upright, magnified}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: The figure places first minima of a single-slit pattern at y=±6 mm. If the slit width doubles with wavelength and screen distance unchanged, what is the new full central maximum width?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 6 mm.
Given: \(y_1=\pm6\ \mathrm{mm};\quad a\to2a;\quad\lambda,\ D\ \text{unchanged}\)
Formula/Principle: \(a\sin\theta=\lambda\Rightarrow y_1=\dfrac{\lambda D}{a};\quad\text{central width}=2y_1\)
Step 1: \(y_1'=\dfrac{\lambda D}{2a}=\dfrac{6}{2}=3\ \mathrm{mm}\)
Worked derivation: \[\text{width}'=2\times3=6\ \mathrm{mm}\]
Check: \[\text{original width}=2\times6=12\ \mathrm{mm};\quad\frac{12}{2}=6\ \mathrm{mm}\]
Why: \(\text{width}\propto\dfrac1a\)
Why not the others: (A) \(3\ \mathrm{mm}=y_1'\) (half-width); (C) \(12\ \mathrm{mm}\) (unchanged); (D) \(24\ \mathrm{mm}\) (\(\text{width}\propto a\)).
Key point: \(\text{central maximum width}=\dfrac{2\lambda D}{a}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.question: A metal emits at 400 nm with stopping potential 1.0 V but not at 600 nm. With hc=1240 eV·nm, find work function and threshold wavelength.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 2.10 eV, ≈590 nm.
Given: \(\lambda=400\ \mathrm{nm},\quad V_s=1.0\ \mathrm V,\quad hc=1240\ \mathrm{eV\,nm}\)
Formula/Principle: \(eV_s=\dfrac{hc}{\lambda}-\phi,\quad\lambda_0=\dfrac{hc}{\phi}\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac{hc}{\lambda}=\dfrac{1240}{400}=3.10\ \mathrm{eV}\)
Step 2: \(\phi=3.10-1.0=2.10\ \mathrm{eV}\)
Worked derivation: \[\lambda_0=\frac{1240}{2.10}\approx590\ \mathrm{nm}\]
Check: \[600\ \mathrm{nm}>590\ \mathrm{nm}\Rightarrow\frac{1240}{600}=2.07\ \mathrm{eV}<\phi\ (\text{no emission})\]
Why: \(K_{\max}=eV_s\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\phi=3.10\ \mathrm{eV}\) (\(eV_s\) not subtracted); (C) \(\phi=1.0\ \mathrm{eV}=eV_s\); (D) \(3.10+1.0=4.10\ \mathrm{eV}\) (sign).
Key point: \(\phi=\dfrac{hc}{\lambda}-eV_s\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: Two identical p-n diodes have equal series resistors on the same DC supply. X has p-side at higher potential; Y has n-side at higher potential. Before breakdown, which comparison holds?
options: A) X conducts appreciably; Y has small reverse current
C) Y conducts appreciably; X is reverse biased
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) X conducts appreciably; Y has small reverse current.
Given: \(X:\ V_p>V_n;\quad Y:\ V_n>V_p;\quad\text{same }R,\ \text{same supply }V\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{forward: }I\approx\dfrac{V-V_D}{R};\quad\text{reverse: }I\approx I_0\ (\mu\mathrm A)\)
Step 1: \(X:\ V_p>V_n\Rightarrow\text{forward bias}\Rightarrow\text{barrier lowered}\)
Step 2: \(Y:\ V_n>V_p\Rightarrow\text{reverse bias}\Rightarrow\text{barrier raised}\)
Worked derivation: \[I_X\approx\frac{V-V_D}{R}\gg I_Y\approx I_0\]
Check: \[V=5\ \mathrm V,\ R=1\ \mathrm{k\Omega},\ V_D=0.7\ \mathrm V:\ I_X=4.3\ \mathrm{mA};\quad I_Y\sim\mu\mathrm A\]
Why: \(\text{forward bias narrows the depletion layer; reverse bias widens it}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(I_X\gg I_Y\); (C) \(X:\ V_p>V_n\ \text{is forward, not reverse}\); (D) \(I_X\ne0\).
Key point: \(\text{p-side positive}=\text{forward bias}\)
